citeAs: Cheng, G., Han, J., & Lu, X. (2017). Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification: Benchmark and State of the Art. Proceedings of the IEEE.
creator: Gong Cheng, Junwei Han, Xiaoqiang Lu (Northwestern Polytechnical University)
description: NWPU-RESISC45 is a large-scale benchmark dataset for Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification (RESISC), created by Northwestern Polytechnical University (NWPU). It contains 31,500 images covering 45 scene classes with 700 images per class, each of size 256×256 pixels in RGB color space. The dataset features rich image variations in translation, spatial resolution, viewpoint, object pose, illumination, background, and occlusion, and covers more than 100 countries and regions worldwide.
name: NWPU-RESISC45
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Scene classes were selected in two steps: (1) investigating all scene classes of existing datasets to form 30 widely-used scene categories; (2) searching keywords such as "OBIA", "GEOBIA", "land cover classification", "land use classification", "geographic image retrieval", and "geospatial object detection" on Web of Science and Google Scholar to carefully select 15 additional meaningful scene classes, resulting in 45 total scene classes. Images were extracted and labeled by experts in the field of remote sensing image interpretation.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was deliberately designed to include high within-class diversity and between-class similarity to avoid saturation of accuracy seen in prior datasets. Fine-grained scene classes with high semantic overlapping were added (e.g., circular farmland vs. rectangular farmland, commercial area vs. industrial area, basketball court vs. tennis court). Images cover more than 100 countries and regions worldwide, including developing, transition, and highly developed economies, to improve geographic diversity.
rai:dataCollection: Images were extracted by experts in the field of remote sensing image interpretation from Google Earth (Google Inc.), which maps the Earth by superimposition of images obtained from satellite imagery, aerial photography, and geographic information system (GIS) onto a 3D globe. The 31,500 images cover more than 100 countries and regions all over the world, including developing, transition, and highly developed economies. Images were carefully selected under all kinds of weathers, seasons, illumination conditions, imaging conditions, and scales.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Satellite imagery, aerial photography, and geographic information system (GIS) data accessed via Google Earth (Google Inc.). Images span spatial resolutions from approximately 30 m to 0.2 m per pixel for most scene classes.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that almost all scene classification methods rely on only traditional remote sensing (overhead imagery) to distinguish different types of land-cover. The dataset does not incorporate ground-level photos or social media geo-tagged data, which could provide complementary information. Some scene classes (island, lake, mountain, and snowberg) have lower spatial resolutions than the stated range of ~30 m to 0.2 m.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were extracted as 256×256 pixel patches in the RGB color space from Google Earth imagery. The spatial resolution varies from about 30 m to 0.2 m per pixel for most scene classes (with lower spatial resolutions for island, lake, mountain, and snowberg classes).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables the development of intelligent earth observation systems for remote sensing image scene classification, with applications in natural hazards detection, land use and land cover determination, environment monitoring, and urban planning. By providing a large-scale publicly available benchmark, it facilitates the development of deep learning methods that can advance the state of the art in remote sensing analysis.
rai:dataUseCases: Remote sensing image scene classification, land use and land cover (LULC) determination, natural hazards detection, geospatial object detection, geographic image retrieval, vegetation mapping, environment monitoring, and urban planning. The dataset is intended to enable the community to develop and evaluate various data-driven algorithms, especially deep learning-based methods.
